entries.title: Are your bones alive?
entries.answer: A dried bone in a museum can make it seem as if bones are just hard sticks. Inside you, each bone contains living cells. Blood travels through small channels to bring those cells supplies. The firm outer layer holds up well under pressure. Toward the inside of many bones, thin pieces of bone form a network with gaps between them. Bone cells slowly take away old bone and build fresh bone as you live.
facts: Some bone has an open pattern that looks a little like a sponge.

questions.text: What jobs do all the bones do together?
Why do some bones have a soft center?
How does blood reach living tissue?

entries.title: How can you tell which things are farther away?
entries.answer: Hold two fingers up with one a little in front of the other. Look with one eye and then with the other. Their positions may seem to change against the wall because each eye sees from a different spot. Your brain can use that difference to judge which object is closer. It has other clues too. A nearby object may hide part of a farther one, and two things you know are the same size may look smaller at different distances.
facts: Distance can be estimated from several different kinds of clues.

questions.text: What turns light from an object into signals the brain can use?
Where else does your brain combine more than one kind of clue?
What organ makes sense of messages traveling from both eyes?

entries.title: How can your eyes tell colors apart?
entries.answer: Many people have three kinds of cone cell near the back of each eye. Each kind reacts most strongly to a different range of light. When you look at an object, more than one kind can respond. Your brain can use that mix to help tell a red marker from a green leaf. People can differ in the way their eyes or brain use these signals. The colors one person can tell apart may be hard for someone else to distinguish.
facts: The three common types of cone cell respond to overlapping ranges of light.

questions.text: How can three kinds of light make a screen look like it has many colors?
Why are colors harder to see at night?
What can give the light that reaches your eyes different colors?

entries.title: How do capillaries deliver oxygen to cells?
entries.answer: The larger blood vessels branch into tiny tubes called capillaries. Each tube has a very thin wall. That lets oxygen and some other materials leave the blood and reach nearby cells. Some things move the other way. Carbon dioxide can travel from cells into the blood, which later brings it to the lungs. A whole network of tiny capillaries keeps most cells close to a place where these exchanges can take place.
facts: Many capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells go through them one at a time.

questions.text: How does blood reach and leave capillaries?
What material carries the oxygen through a capillary?
Where does oxygen first get into blood?

entries.title: How do groups of cells do bigger jobs?
entries.answer: A single cell can send a message, move, or carry a supply, but a large body needs many cells working in groups. A group of organized cells and the material around them forms a tissue. Muscle tissue can pull together to make a large move. Another kind of tissue makes a cover, like the layer that lines the inside of your mouth. Several different tissues can join to make an organ with more than one job.
facts: Several kinds of tissue can work together inside a single organ.

questions.text: What are the little living units that tissues contain?
What are some jobs done by the tissues in your skin?
How can an organ use muscle tissue to do a job?

entries.title: How do joints let your body move?
entries.answer: A joint is a place where bones meet. Many joints let one bone move against the other. A layer of smooth cartilage covers the touching ends in a freely moving joint. Liquid in the joint helps the surfaces slide. Strong strips called ligaments keep the bones from moving too far apart. Different joints allow different moves. Elbows mainly bend and straighten, while the joints in your shoulders let your arms move in many directions.
facts: Your elbow mainly bends and straightens like a hinge.

questions.text: What pulls on the bones at a joint?
Which joints let a bone swing in many directions?
What helps moving bones slide past each other?

entries.title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
entries.answer: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs. Oxygen from the air passes through the thin walls of those sacs and into the blood. A gas called carbon dioxide moves the other way, from blood into the sacs. When you breathe out, some of that carbon dioxide leaves your body. Your heart keeps sending blood past the sacs so it can pick up oxygen.

sections.heading: The muscle underneath
sections.text: A broad muscle called the diaphragm moves down when it tightens, making more room in your chest so air flows into the lungs.

facts: The tiny air sacs are called alveoli.
The left lung is a little smaller than the right, leaving room for the heart.

questions.text: How does oxygen-rich blood travel around the body?
What material does your digestive system put into blood?
What part of the body controls how fast we breathe?

entries.title: How do muscles move your bones?
entries.answer: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones. A muscle can shorten and pull, a bit like someone tugging a rope. It cannot push the bone back the other way. To straighten your elbow, a muscle toward the back of your upper arm can pull in another direction. Muscles throughout your body work together to help you stand upright, pick things up, and move without toppling over.
facts: The biceps helps bend the elbow.
The triceps helps straighten the elbow.

questions.text: Where do the signals for a planned movement come from?
Why is the heart’s squeeze important?
How can a bar that turns about a point make a task easier?

entries.title: How do red blood cells carry oxygen?
entries.answer: A red blood cell is a flexible, flat disc with thinner spots in its middle. It carries a substance called hemoglobin. When the blood passes through your lungs, oxygen can attach to hemoglobin. Farther along, oxygen can come loose and move from the blood toward cells that need it. Hemoglobin contains iron and gives the red cells their color. The cells can bend as they squeeze through some very narrow blood vessels.
facts: A mature human red blood cell usually lasts about four months.

questions.text: Where does a red cell pick up oxygen?
Where are fresh blood cells made?
Which tiny tubes bring red cells close to other cells?

entries.title: How do taste buds tell flavors apart?
entries.answer: When you take a bite, tiny bits of dissolved food meet taste cells. Groups of such cells form taste buds. Signals from those cells help your brain notice tastes such as sweet, bitter, or sour. Flavor includes more than these signals. The smell of food, its warmth, and how it feels in your mouth matter too. With a stuffy nose you may still taste the sweetness in a piece of fruit but have a harder time telling which fruit it is.
facts: Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savory are five well-known kinds of taste.

questions.text: How does the nose help you tell foods apart?
What happens to food after you taste and swallow it?
How can mouth feel change what you think of as flavor?

entries.title: How do you feel rough and smooth things?
entries.answer: Try brushing a finger over paper, a sweater, or the top of a table. The push on the skin changes as your finger travels over tiny bumps. Special nerve endings pick up these tiny changes. Signals move from the finger toward the brain, which puts them together to help you feel a texture. Your skin also has ways to notice heat, cold, and stronger pressure. These different signals help you feel more than just whether something is touching you.
facts: Different kinds of nerve endings help you feel pressure, warmth, cold, or vibration.

questions.text: Where are the nerve endings that detect many touches?
How do readers use touch to tell patterns apart?
Where do most touch messages go to be understood?

entries.title: How do you smell something nearby?
entries.answer: A bowl of cut oranges can smell fresh from across a table. Some molecules leave the fruit and move through the air. When air flows through your nose, a few reach a small patch of cells high inside it. Those cells can notice certain molecules and send signals to your brain. The brain uses the pattern of signals to recognize a smell. Odors from food can also reach the same spot through the back of your mouth.
facts: Air can carry scent molecules from a food you have never touched.

questions.text: What senses work together to make a flavor?
What makes sense of messages from your nose?
How can pieces of matter small enough to go unseen reach your nose?

entries.title: How do your ears hear?
entries.answer: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move. Three tiny bones carry the movement farther into the ear. It makes waves in liquid inside the cochlea, a spiral-shaped part of the inner ear. Tiny hair cells respond to this motion and help turn it into signals. A nerve carries those signals to your brain. Your brain makes sense of them as sounds, such as a dog barking or a bell ringing.

sections.heading: Different pitches
sections.text: Different parts of the cochlea respond especially well to different pitches, from a deep drum to a high whistle.

facts: The three tiny bones are in the middle ear.
The cochlea is filled with fluid.

questions.text: How do nerve cells carry the messages your ear starts?
How does air movement become a sound wave?
How does a bat use returning sounds to find its way?

entries.title: How do your eyes help you see?
entries.answer: Light from the world enters your eye through a round opening. Clear parts near the front bend the light so it makes a sharp picture on a layer at the back. That layer is the retina. Some of its cells change incoming light into messages. A bundle of nerve fibers carries them toward your brain. Your brain combines messages from both eyes and helps you recognize the shapes, colors, and motions around you.
facts: Your retina lines the inside of the back of the eye.

questions.text: How does the eye let in more or less light?
Where does light entering the eye come from?
What turns messages from the eye into what you see?

entries.title: How do your fingernails grow?
entries.answer: Your fingernail grows from a group of cells under the skin near the base of the nail. These cells make new nail material that slowly pushes older nail forward. The part you can trim has hardened with a tough protein called keratin. It has no nerves, which is why clipping just the free edge does not hurt. A nail protects the tender tip of your finger and gives it a firmer edge for picking things up.
facts: The visible part of a nail grows forward as new material is made near its base.

questions.text: How does skin also replace its outer surface?
What other parts of the body are made of tough keratin?
How do fingertips sense the texture of a small object?

entries.title: How does your blood plug a cut?
entries.answer: If a tiny vessel is damaged, its walls can squeeze inward to slow the flow. Small bits of cells called platelets stick to the broken spot and to each other. Their group makes a plug. The blood can also produce a mesh of threads that strengthens the plug. Together these steps form a clot, which keeps more blood from escaping while the vessel and nearby skin begin to repair themselves.
facts: Platelets are pieces that break off from much larger cells.

questions.text: Which liquid carries platelets around the body?
Where are the cells that make platelets?
What other work does skin do to protect you?

entries.title: How does your body keep its balance?
entries.answer: Your brain checks several clues to see whether you are upright or tipping. Eyes can tell you how the room is moving in your view. Sensors in muscles and joints report how bent or stretched a body part is. Small parts of the inner ear detect a turn or tilt of your head. Your brain blends these signals and tells your muscles to adjust. That is how you can stay up when the ground is uneven.
facts: Tiny canals in your inner ear help sense turns of your head.

questions.text: What other jobs do parts of the inner ear do?
How do your eyes tell you the room is moving in your view?
What makes the small movements that keep you from tipping?

entries.title: How does your brain send messages?
entries.answer: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron. Electrical signals travel along a neuron, and chemical messengers can pass information across tiny gaps to other cells. Signals from your eyes help your brain work out where the pencil is. Signals from your brain and spinal cord help tell your arm and hand muscles how to move. Neurons also take part in things such as remembering a story or hearing a friend say your name.

sections.heading: Parts have different jobs
sections.text: Areas near the back of your brain help make sense of what you see. Other areas help plan movement, process sound, or remember what happened.

facts: The spinal cord carries many messages between the brain and body.
Your brain does jobs you do not have to think about, including helping control your breathing.

questions.text: What happens after a sound reaches your ear?
How does your body pull on bones to move your hand?
What happens when the brain tells breathing muscles to move?

entries.title: How does your brain talk to hormone glands?
entries.answer: A tiny gland under your brain is called the pituitary. A nearby part of your brain helps tell it what to release. Several of its messages travel in your blood and tell other glands how much to work. Others help direct growth or help your kidneys manage water. Picture a group of people passing notes. The brain can send a note to the pituitary, which then passes a message to the right place.
facts: The pituitary is roughly the size of a pea.

questions.text: How do brain cells send other kinds of messages?
Which neck gland responds to messages from the pituitary?
What organs adjust how much water your body holds?

entries.title: How does your heart move blood?
entries.answer: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist. The right side sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends that blood out to the rest of your body. Each side has a room where blood arrives and another room that pushes blood out. Small flaps called valves open and close so the blood keeps moving in the right direction.

sections.heading: Two trips, one pump
sections.text: Blood returning from the body takes a short trip through the lungs, then comes back to the heart for the trip around the body.

facts: The heart has four chambers.
An electrical signal helps time each beat.

questions.text: Where does blood pick up oxygen?
What takes some waste and extra water out of blood?
What sends signals to move other muscles?

quiz.question: Where does the right side of your heart send blood next?
quiz.explanation: The right side sends blood to the lungs, where the blood can pick up oxygen.

entries.title: How does your rib cage protect you?
entries.answer: Your ribs curve around your chest like a long set of hoops. At the back they join the spine. Many also connect to the breastbone at the front, either directly or through other pieces of cartilage. The cage helps guard soft parts inside it, including your lungs and heart. It still moves. Some muscles between the ribs lift the chest as you breathe in, helping make more room inside.
facts: Most people have twelve pairs of ribs.

questions.text: Why does making room for your lungs help you breathe?
What does the heart do inside that cage?
Where do the ribs connect in your back?

entries.title: What are arteries and veins?
entries.answer: Blood takes a trip through tubes called blood vessels. An artery carries blood away from the heart. The largest ones have tough walls and can stretch a bit with each beat. A vein carries blood back to the heart. Many veins, especially in arms and legs, have little flaps that help stop blood moving backward. The direction the blood moves makes a vessel an artery or a vein.
facts: Some veins have flaps that help keep blood from slipping backward.

questions.text: What gives blood the push it needs to travel?
What connects the smallest arteries and veins?
Which organs receive blood from the heart to trade gases?

entries.title: What causes the pulse you can feel?
entries.answer: Every time your heart sends blood out, the push makes a small wave of pressure travel through your arteries. You may notice that push as a beat in a place where an artery passes close to your skin, such as near your wrist. The wave goes along the tubes, a little like a squeeze making a bump travel along a full hose. Your heartbeat starts the wave, though the pulse you feel may be far from the heart.
facts: A pulse is easier to feel where an artery runs close to the surface of the skin.

questions.text: What starts the wave that you feel in an artery?
How does an artery differ from a vein?
Why might the heart work harder when muscles are active?

entries.title: What do white blood cells do?
entries.answer: White blood cells are part of your body’s defenses. There are several kinds with different jobs. Some can surround and break down tiny invaders or bits of dead cells. Other kinds help the body recognize things it has met before. The cells can travel in blood and can also move into the surrounding tissue. On most days you never notice them, even though they are busy checking what is happening around you.
facts: White blood cells can leave the blood and move into nearby tissues.

questions.text: What else travels through the blood?
Where does the body make new blood cells?
What barrier helps block harmful things before white cells are needed?

entries.title: What do your kidneys do?
entries.answer: Your kidneys help keep the right mix of water, salts, and other materials in your blood. Inside each kidney, tiny filters take some water and small materials out of blood. The kidneys then send much of the water and useful materials back. Extra water and some waste leave the kidneys as urine. Thin tubes carry urine to the bladder, where it stays until you pee. These filters work all day, even when you are sleeping or thinking about something else.

sections.heading: A filter plus a return trip
sections.text: A nephron is one of the kidney’s tiny working units. It includes a filter and a tube that gives the body a chance to take back useful material.

facts: Most people have two kidneys.
A healthy kidney has about a million nephrons.

questions.text: What keeps blood moving to the kidneys and back?
Which digestive organ takes up water from leftover food?
Where does the body get rid of a waste gas?

entries.title: What does a gallbladder do?
entries.answer: Your gallbladder is a little pouch tucked under your liver. As the liver makes bile, some of that liquid goes to the pouch and stays there between meals. When you eat, the pouch can squeeze bile through small tubes into the first part of your small intestine. There, bile helps spread fat into smaller droplets. The smaller drops give the body’s digestive juices more surface to work on.
facts: The gallbladder fits against the underside of the liver.

questions.text: Which organ makes the bile first?
What happens to food in the small intestine?
What other juices help break down food?

entries.title: What does bone marrow do?
entries.answer: Deep inside some bones is soft material called marrow. Red marrow is a place where new blood cells are made. Among them are red blood cells that carry oxygen and white blood cells that help protect the body. It also makes the large cells that shed little pieces called platelets. Those pieces help stop bleeding. Yellow marrow has much more fat. Even though marrow sits inside bone, it has a supply of blood moving through it.
facts: The inside of an adult bone can contain red or yellow marrow.

questions.text: Why does your blood need red cells?
How do platelets help seal a cut?
What makes bone a living part of you?

entries.title: What does the thyroid do?
entries.answer: The thyroid is a small gland near the front of your neck. It makes hormones, which are messages that move in your blood. The messages from your thyroid help tune how fast many parts of your body use energy. Thyroid hormones also help with normal growth and development. The gland needs a little of the element iodine to make these messages. It is often drawn with two halves that look like butterfly wings.
facts: The thyroid lies near the front of the neck and has a butterfly-like shape.

questions.text: Which other organ can send messages through your blood?
What small gland helps tell the thyroid when to work?
What do people mean when they say something uses energy?

entries.title: What does your liver do?
entries.answer: Your liver sits mostly on the right side of your belly, beneath the ribs. Blood from much of your digestive system brings it materials from food. The liver can store some supplies, change others into forms the body can use, and help handle waste. It also makes bile, a liquid that helps the small intestine handle fat. Many of these jobs happen at once, all without you having to think about them.
facts: The liver makes bile, which helps your body use fats from food.

questions.text: Where do nutrients in food enter your body?
Where can the body store the bile the liver makes?
How does the body carry nutrients to its organs?

entries.title: What does your skin do?
entries.answer: Skin forms a cover that helps keep water in your body and keeps many harmful things out. The surface can get scuffed, so new cells push up from below to replace old ones. A deeper layer contains tiny blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, and the places where hairs begin. Your skin also senses what touches you. It is a living organ, and its jobs include protection, touch, and keeping your body from getting too hot.
facts: The outer layer of your skin continually sheds and replaces cells.

questions.text: What helps skin tell rough from smooth?
How does skin cool your body?
What hard parts grow from skin near your fingertips?

entries.title: What does your skull protect?
entries.answer: Your skull is made of several bones that fit together. Some form a strong case around your brain. Others shape your face, hold your eyes, or help support your teeth. Most of the skull stays still when you chew. Your lower jaw moves at joints near your ears. In a baby, the bones around the brain have spaces between them. These spaces help the skull grow and close gradually.
facts: The seams between some bones of the skull are called sutures.

questions.text: What happens inside the brain the skull protects?
Which column of bones protects the spinal cord?
What other bones shelter organs?

entries.title: What does your spine do?
entries.answer: Your spine is a column made mostly of individual bones called vertebrae. Many of them are separated by firm pads that cushion the bones and allow a little movement. When a lot of small moves add up, you can bend your back. Inside the column is a passage that helps protect your spinal cord. Alongside the spine, nerves branch out to carry messages between your brain and many parts of your body.
facts: The pads between many vertebrae are called discs.

questions.text: How does your full skeleton support you?
Which bones protect the brain the spine connects to?
Where do messages going down the spinal cord start?

entries.title: What is blood made of?
entries.answer: Blood has a liquid part called plasma. It is mostly water and carries things such as dissolved nutrients and waste. Riding in it are several kinds of cells and cell pieces. Red blood cells carry oxygen. Different kinds of white blood cells help the body notice and respond to trouble. Bits called platelets help make plugs when a small blood vessel breaks. Blood has so many red cells that the mixture looks red.
facts: Plasma makes up a little over half the volume of typical blood.

questions.text: What pushes blood around your body?
Why does blood look red?
Which blood cells help defend your body?

entries.title: What is cartilage?
entries.answer: Feel the end of your nose. It can bend a little without flopping. A tough, springy material called cartilage helps give it shape. Your outer ears contain cartilage too. The cartilage on the ends of many bones has a different job. Its surface is smooth, so it helps the bones slide in a moving joint. The ribs also meet cartilage at the front of your chest, which allows some movement as you breathe.
facts: A smooth type of cartilage covers the ends of bones in many moving joints.

questions.text: Why is cartilage useful in a bending knee?
How is a hard bone built?
Where does cartilage help shape your chest?

entries.title: What makes little bumps rise on your skin?
entries.answer: You might see rows of little bumps on your arm in the cold, or while listening to exciting music. Each bump can happen when a tiny muscle tugs at a hair near its base. The hair can rise a little, and the skin around it can bunch up. In animals with a thick coat, standing hairs can trap more air. For a person’s short arm hairs the change is often easiest to notice as small raised spots.
facts: Small muscles attached to hairs make goosebumps rise.

questions.text: What part of skin holds the base of an individual hair?
How does the skin help with the opposite problem of getting too warm?
What other actions can happen before you decide to do them?

entries.title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
entries.answer: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it. After you swallow, muscles squeeze food down a tube to your stomach. There it gets churned together with digestive juices. The mixture then moves into your small intestine. There, more juices break food into tiny pieces your body can use, and most nutrients pass out through the intestine wall. Your large intestine takes up water from what is left, and some of the leftovers eventually leave your body as poop.

sections.heading: Food moves even when you lie down
sections.text: Muscles in the wall of the food tube squeeze in waves. This helps push swallowed food along, even when gravity is not pulling it straight down.

facts: The food tube is called the esophagus.
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.

questions.text: How do nutrients travel after they enter the blood?
How does your body get rid of some wastes through urine?
What other body system takes in something we need to live?

entries.title: Where does hair grow from?
entries.answer: A hair gets longer from the end hidden inside the skin. That end sits in a small pocket called a follicle. Living cells near the bottom add material. By the time the hair sticks out from your head, it is mainly a strand of hardened protein. There are no nerves in that part, so a haircut does not hurt. Hairs may grow for a time, rest, then fall out as the cycle starts again.
facts: Each growing hair starts in a pocket in skin called a follicle.

questions.text: What other hard part grows from cells near its base?
What else is found under the surface of skin?
How do eyelashes and tears help take care of your eyes?

entries.title: Why can your body react before you decide?
entries.answer: Pulling your hand away from a hot surface can happen before you have time to plan to move. Nerves on the skin send a message inward. Along some routes, a message can pass through the spinal cord and turn on muscles right away. Other messages reach the brain too, so you notice what happened. A quick automatic response like this is called a reflex. Your body does not need to work out a longer plan for every quick change around it.
facts: Some reflexes pass through the spinal cord before a person is aware of the event.

questions.text: How does the brain use messages to help control motion?
What helps the body notice what touches your skin?
Where is the spinal cord protected?

entries.title: Why can your shoulder move in so many directions?
entries.answer: At your shoulder, the rounded top of your upper arm bone fits into a socket. Imagine a ball resting in a shallow cup. A round surface can turn in more directions than a door hinge, so you can lift your arm, sweep it forward, or make a circle. Your hip has the same general shape, but its deeper socket fits tightly around the round top of the thigh bone and helps support your weight.
facts: Your hip and shoulder both have ball-and-socket joints.

questions.text: How do the parts of a moving joint work together?
What pulls your arm into a new position?
How do bones move without rubbing roughly?

entries.title: Why do children lose their first teeth?
entries.answer: A child’s first set of teeth fits into a small jaw. As the jaw grows, many of these teeth have to make room for a later set. The root that held a first tooth gradually becomes smaller. When little of it is left to hold the tooth, the part above the gums can wobble and eventually come out. A permanent tooth may have been growing under it. Not every new tooth takes the place of an old one. Some come in at the back.
facts: People usually get 20 baby teeth.

questions.text: Why are some of your teeth shaped like small cutters and others like grinders?
What covers the part of a tooth above your gums?
What bones support your teeth?

entries.title: Why do you have a pancreas?
entries.answer: The pancreas is a flat organ behind the stomach. It makes liquids containing helpers called enzymes. The liquid flows to the small intestine, where enzymes split food into smaller bits. The pancreas has a second job too. It releases messages called hormones into your blood. One of them is insulin, which helps many cells take in sugar from the blood. One organ can help with both the food in your gut and what travels in your blood.
facts: The pancreas sends digestive juices to the first part of the small intestine.

questions.text: What happens after food reaches the small intestine?
What other liquid goes into the intestine to help digest fats?
What is another gland that makes messages for the blood?

entries.title: Why do you need a skeleton?
entries.answer: Your skeleton gives your body shape and holds it up when you stand. It gives muscles something firm to pull on when you run, wave, or chew. Some parts act like a shield. Your skull surrounds your brain, and your ribs curve around your heart and lungs. A skeleton does more than hold you together. Bones store minerals, and soft tissue inside some bones helps make new blood cells.
facts: A typical adult skeleton has 206 bones.

questions.text: Where do bones meet so you can move?
Which bones protect your lungs?
What does the soft material inside some bones do?

entries.title: Why do your eyes make tears?
entries.answer: Your eyes need a thin coat of liquid for more than crying. Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the eye. That layer keeps the surface moist and helps it stay smooth. Tears can also wash loose dust away. Some drain through small openings in the corners of your eyes and travel down into your nose. When you cry, there may be more tears than those openings can drain, so some run down your cheeks.
facts: Some tears drain into the nose through tear ducts.

questions.text: Why do your eyes need a smooth, clear front surface?
What part changes the amount of light entering the eye?
How do tiny hairs around your eyes help protect them?

entries.title: Why do your pupils change size?
entries.answer: Walk from a sunny yard into a dim room and your eyes start to adjust. The small dark opening in each eye is its pupil. A ring around it, the iris, contains muscles that can make the opening wider or narrower. A wider opening lets more light in when it is dark. In brighter light, a narrower opening limits how much enters. The change happens without needing to think about it.
facts: The pupil is an opening. The iris around it is the colored part of the eye.

questions.text: What happens to light after it enters the pupil?
What is the light that enters your eye?
What keeps the front surface of the eye smooth?

entries.title: Why do your teeth have different shapes?
entries.answer: When you bite an apple, a flat tooth near the front can cut off a thin piece. The pointier teeth beside the front ones can help hold or tear what you bite. Farther back, broad teeth can crush and grind food as your jaw closes. These shapes do similar jobs to different kitchen tools, though all the teeth work together. Chewing also mixes small pieces with saliva, which helps them move on toward the rest of digestion.
facts: Wide grinding teeth sit toward the back of your mouth.

questions.text: Why is chewing one of the first parts of digestion?
What happens to your teeth as your mouth grows?
What protects the outside of all these shapes when you chew?

entries.title: Why does sweating cool you down?
entries.answer: Your body can make sweat when you get warm. The sweat spreads across your skin. As its water changes into a gas and mixes with the air, the change takes some heat from your skin. This cooling works best when the sweat can evaporate, rather than just roll off you. On a muggy day, the air already carries plenty of water, so sweat often evaporates more slowly and you may stay sweaty longer.
facts: Sweat glands send moisture to the skin through tiny openings.

questions.text: Which layers contain sweat glands?
Where else does liquid water change into a gas?
How can you sense that something is warm?

entries.title: Why is it hard to see colors in the dark?
entries.answer: Look at colorful things in a bright room and then in the same room after it gets dim. You may still make out shapes after a while, but colors are harder to notice. Small parts of the retina called rod cells are good at detecting weak light. Cone cells help tell colors apart when there is enough light to use them well. In very dim light, rod cells do much more of the work, so fine details and colors can be harder to see.
facts: Rod cells can help you see in light too dim for strong color vision.
